extracted.intended_audience: writers and readers of queer romance
extracted.subtask_description: Advice and reflective guidance for authors writing queer romance (rom-coms and uplifting love stories) focused on representation, tone, setting, and reader needs. Emphasizes creating safe, joyful, and authentic queer-centered narratives.

rubrics_metrics.name: Queer characters are centered and not sidelined
rubrics_metrics.description: Queer characters are centered and not sidelined.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The author emphasizes making the protagonist queer and placing queer relationships front and center rather than treating them as background or token. Examples: having a protagonist the author relates to, a love interest they fancy, and friendship groups that feel real. This includes writing a straight best friend in a way that supports—rather than eclipses—the queer lead.

rubrics_metrics.name: Create safe spaces in the story/world
rubrics_metrics.description: I want readers to feel that when they’re with my characters, in my hands, they can relax. It’s a safe space.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Intentionally craft settings and community dynamics that offer kindness and acceptance (even when those settings may not mirror real-world inclusivity). Example: inventing a welcoming 'queer commune' in a rural village so readers can escape into a world where characters are met with acceptance. Purpose: give readers solace and a place to 'relax into' the narrative.

rubrics_metrics.name: Portray queer joy and shamelessness
rubrics_metrics.description: Part of the joy for me as a queer woman, when writing about characters falling for each other, is the shamelessness of it all—the pain and the pleasure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Celebrate queer desire, crushes, and romantic pleasure openly rather than coding them in secrecy or shame. Bring into the light experiences that were historically hidden. Use scenes of swooning, crushes, and unabashed romantic feeling to normalize joy and make the emotional stakes pleasurable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Write what you know / authenticity of voice
rubrics_metrics.description: I wrote about what I knew—I wrote what I wanted to read.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ground stories in lived experience or empathically rendered understanding so characters and relationships feel real. This can mean depicting recognizable twenty- and thirty-something queer experiences, friendship dynamics, workplace romances, or other familiar social textures. Authenticity includes pleasurable small details and emotional truth rather than relying solely on plot mechanics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provide a clear guarantee of representation so readers can relax
rubrics_metrics.description: I think that romance/rom coms are a proper comfort read for me, but that is compromised if I spend the whole book hoping for/searching for queer characters or positive/properly researched queer rep by straight authors! Sometimes I just need an absolute guarantee before I start reading that that isn’t something I’m going to be worrying about, so that I can just properly relax into reading.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Signal representation clearly (through marketing, blurbs, categories, or early textual cues) so readers who need queer-centered stories know they will get them. Avoid ambiguous portrayals that force readers to 'search' for whether the book safely contains the representation they seek.

rubrics_metrics.name: Properly researched and positive queer representation; avoid shallow hints
rubrics_metrics.description: Search for/positive/properly researched queer rep by straight authors!
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Especially for non-queer authors, research and care are required to render queer characters respectfully and accurately. Avoid relying on vague hints or stereotypes; aim for believable, respectful portrayals that feel researched and not performative. The warning in the text: poorly researched or ambiguous rep undermines comfort reading for queer readers.

rubrics_metrics.name: A single book does not have to represent all queer people
rubrics_metrics.description: We’re getting to a place where one queer book does not have to represent every queer person.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Encourage a plurality of queer stories and acknowledge diversity within queer communities; avoid treating any single narrative as definitive. This criterion supports publishing many varied queer voices so different readers can find reflections that resonate without burdening one text with universal representation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Queer romance as comfort reads—uplift, solace, happy endings
rubrics_metrics.description: I’d written a comfort read, a story that made people laugh and cry and believe in love and want to hug their friends.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When aiming for comfort fiction, emphasize uplifting tones, emotional payoffs, humor, and satisfying romantic arcs (often including hopeful or happy endings). The goal is to provide readers with relief, joy, and emotional satisfaction rather than persistent trauma or unresolved harm.

rubrics_metrics.name: Depict authentic crushes and emotional complexity
rubrics_metrics.description: I love having a crush. Sometimes I feel it coming like a wave... Sometimes I feel a crush coming like a flood, immediate and catastrophic.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Show the range of crush experiences—from tender, prolonged longing to immediate, overwhelming obsession—so romantic feelings feel true and varied. Include both ecstatic and anxious reactions (e.g., daydreaming, melodrama, self-pity) to render emotional texture and relatability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Include believable friendships and community support
rubrics_metrics.description: Friendship groups that made sense. I took great pleasure in writing a straight best friend.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Portray supportive friendships and found-family dynamics that feel organic and contribute to the protagonist’s emotional life. Community representation (and how booksellers/librarians frame/display such books) can help readers feel included and safer; consider group dynamics and social networks as central to the story’s emotional economy.
